items.prompt: White to move. Tap every square the bishop on c1 can move to.

claims.statement: The bishop on c1 can go to exactly these five squares.

hints: Bishops move on diagonals. Which diagonal leaves c1 towards the kingside?
The pawn on b2 blocks the other diagonal.
The squares are d2, e3, f4, g5 and one more on the edge.
items.explain: Before d4 the pawn on d2 shut the diagonal; now the whole diagonal to h6 is open. That is what the pawn move prepared.

items.prompt: White to move. Can White castle kingside in this position?
hints: Castling needs the squares between king and rook to be empty.
Which two squares lie between e1 and h1?
The bishop and knight on that side have both moved.
items.explain: The bishop left f1 and the knight left g1, so the squares between king and rook are empty and no square on the way is attacked. Castling is legal.

items.prompt: White to move. May White castle queenside?
hints: Which squares lie between the king on e1 and the rook on a1?
Check b1, c1 and d1.
Each has been emptied by an earlier move.
items.explain: The knight left b1, the bishop left c1 and the queen left d1, and the squares the king crosses are not attacked. Castling queenside is legal.

items.prompt: White to move. May White castle queenside?

claims.statement: Castling queenside is illegal while the queen stands on d1.

hints: Which squares lie between the king on e1 and the rook on a1?
Is any of them occupied?
Look at d1.
items.explain: The queen on d1 stands between king and rook, so castling queenside is not allowed yet. Everything else is as in the previous position; only the queen differs, and one queen move prepares the castling.

items.prompt: Black to move. Find the pawn move that covers b5 and d5 and also leaves c7 free for the queen to retreat to.

claims.statement: After ...c6 one black pawn attacks b5.
After ...c6 the queen on a5 attacks c7, so it can retreat there.
...c6 is within 0.4 pawns of the engine's first choice (depth 16).

hints: Which pawn stands in front of the queen's route back to the king's side?
A pawn on c6 would cover two squares at once.
It is the pawn next to the b-pawn.
items.explain: The c-pawn steps to c6, where it covers b5 and d5 and leaves c7 empty for the queen. A queen retreat to c7 is then one move away. At depth 16 the move is close to the engine's first choice.

items.prompt: Black to move. Tap every square the bishop on f8 can move to.

claims.statement: The bishop on f8 can go to exactly these five squares.

hints: The bishop moves along the diagonal that leaves f8 towards the queenside.
The pawn that stood on e7 has moved.
Count five squares, from e7 to the edge.
items.explain: The pawn on e7 used to block the diagonal. After ...e6 the bishop reaches e7, d6, c5, b4 and a3. A move such as ...Be7 also clears f8 for castling.

items.prompt: Black to move after the knight move to f3. Is the black queen attacked?

claims.statement: No white piece attacks the queen on d5.

hints: Which white pieces could reach d5?
The knight on f3 attacks d4, e5, g5 and h4, among others.
Check d5 against those squares.
items.explain: The knight on f3 does not attack d5 and no other white piece does. Black is not forced to move the queen, which is why this move order gives Black more choice.

items.prompt: Black to move, queen attacked. Which retreat gives exactly the position of the main line (same squares for all pieces)?

claims.statement: The retreats to a5, d6 and d8 are all within 0.4 pawns of the engine's first choice (depth 16).
After the retreat the black queen stands on a5.

hints: Compare this position with the main line: which pieces are on the same squares?
In the main line the queen retreated along a diagonal toward the a-file.
The retreat is to a5.
items.explain: The knights on c3 and f3 and the knight on f6 are all where the main line has them, so Black can choose the same queen square, a5. At depth 16 a5, d6 and d8 are all close to the engine's first choice, so the choice is a matter of plan, not of safety.

items.prompt: Black to move. Choose a developing move for the bishop on c8 that keeps it outside the pawn chain.

claims.statement: ...Bf5 and ...Bg4 are both within 0.4 pawns of the engine's first choice (depth 16).
...e6 here is worse than the best move by at least 0.25 pawns.

hints: The bishop on c8 still has open diagonals.
A bishop is best placed where none of its own pawns blocks it.
Choose a bishop move.
items.explain: Moving the bishop first keeps it outside the chain. Both ...Bf5 and ...Bg4 do that. ...e6 would shut the bishop in, and the engine rates it clearly worse than the bishop moves (at least 0.25 pawns in this check).

feedback_by_move.e7e6: The pawn closes the bishop's diagonal and the bishop is left with one square; the engine rates this clearly worse than a bishop move.

items.prompt: White to move. Pick a sound developing or castling move (not a pawn move).

claims.statement: Bd2, Qe2, Ne5, Nh4 and O-O are each within 0.4 pawns of the engine's first choice (depth 16).

hints: Count White's pieces that are still at home.
A piece move or castling is wanted, not a pawn move.
Several moves are fine; each prepares something different.
items.explain: Bd2 unpins and develops, Qe2 faces the e-file, Ne5 plants a knight in the centre, Nh4 hits the bishop on f5 and O-O brings the king to safety. At depth 16 all five are close to the engine's first choice, so the choice is a matter of plan.

items.prompt: Black to move. Develop the last knight.

claims.statement: ...Nbd7 is within 0.4 pawns of the engine's first choice (depth 16), as is ...e6.

hints: Black has one knight still on the back rank.
Which square does it go to without blocking the bishop?
The square is on the d-file.
items.explain: The knight comes to d7. ...e6 is also fine here (the engine rates the two within 0.4 pawns). The knight move is chosen because the bishop on f5 and the queen are already placed. At depth 16 it is close to the engine's first choice.
